fatal_errors: The proposed sluggish-diffusion, entropy-stabilization mechanism is the opposite of the observed non-sluggish diffusion and kinetically controlled instability.
The hypothesis predicts suppressed segregation and coarsening, whereas Au and Cu segregate to the surface and subsequently melt or evaporate, producing substantial particle-size loss.
A slightly oxidizing environment replaces the target vacuum-heating intervention and introduces oxide kinetics that could dominate the measurements.
The response omits the decisive size- and shape-dependent behavior of sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
No supporting evidence is cited despite claiming support from general theoretical frameworks.
explanation: The response addresses the broad topic of thermal stability and proposes measurable comparisons, but it largely restates the conventional entropy-stabilization baseline that the target study disproves. The target system becomes unstable above roughly 673 K because surface-energy differences drive active Au/Cu diffusion and surface segregation, enhanced by particle reshaping; the segregated shell melts or evaporates near 973 K, causing loss of small particles and about 22% size reduction. The proposed oxidizing experiment could test a generic sluggish-diffusion hypothesis, but oxidation, compositional differences, and oxide passivation would confound attribution to configurational entropy. It also lacks the specified equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt composition, sub-10 nm size regime, vacuum ramp, stepped temperatures, in situ STEM-EDS correlation, and shape-sensitive diffusion analysis.
